12279               	; 	#if NES
12280               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
12281               	; 	'
12282               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
12283               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
12284               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
12285               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
12286               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
12287               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
12288               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
12289               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
12290               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
12291               	; 	'
12292               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
12293               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
12294               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
12295               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
12296               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
12297               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
12298               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
12299               	; 	'
12300               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
12301               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
12302               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
12303               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
12304               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
12305               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
12306               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
12307               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
12308               	; 	' with room to spare.
12309               	; 	'
12310               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
12311               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
12312               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
12313               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
12314               	; 	WAIT
12315               	; 	#endif
12316               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
12317               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them

12319               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
12320               	; 	' 7 an east one.
12321               	; 	'
12322               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
12323               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
12324               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
12325               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
12326               	; 	'
12327               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
12328               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the

12663               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
12664               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
12665               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
12666               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
12667               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
12668               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
12669               	; 	'
12670               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
12671               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
12672               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
12673               	; 	'
12674               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
12675               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
12676               	; 	'   +2  GREY
12677               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
12678               	; 	'
12679               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
12680               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
12681               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
12682               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
12683               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
12684               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
12685               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
12686               	; 	'
12687               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
12688               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
12689               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.

12691               	; 	' The dots are erased by ANDing their bits out, so anything sharing a row
12692               	; 	' with one is rubbed away wherever an actor has passed -- which is why

12963               	; 	'
12964               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
12965               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did

13139               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that

13797               	;
13798               	; #if NES
13799               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
13800               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
13801               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
13802               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
13803               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
13804               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
13805               	; 	'
13806               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
13807               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
13808               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
13809               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
13810               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
13811               	; 	'
13812               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
13813               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
13814               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
13815               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
13816               	; 	'
13817               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
13818               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
13819               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
13820               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
13821               	; 	' these beside it.
13822               	; 	'
13823               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
13824               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
13825               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
13826               	; nes_boxatt:
13827               	; 	' THE RESULT BOX (#nav 9170) IS PPU ROWS 9-11, ONE ATTRIBUTE ROW: its upper
13828               	; 	' quadrants hold the roof slab (row 8) and the box's top row, its lower
13829               	; 	' ones the text and the bottom row. Upper = P3, which is P0 with black
13830               	; 	' swapped for the box's navy, so the slab keeps its green and gold and the
13831               	; 	' top row, drawn in CH_ECAR (solid index 2), is navy; lower = P1, whose
13832               	; 	' paper IS that navy. 95 = P1 under P3, and nothing else is touched.
13833               	; 	'
13834               	; 	' GAME OVER (9178) is PPU rows 14-16: the same 95 on attribute row 3 (P3
13835               	; 	' over rows 12-13, where the counters already use P3; black goes navy
13836               	; 	' there while it is up), and P3 over P0 (15) on row 4 for its navy bottom
13837               	; 	' row. The lower half of row 4 is P0 on every screen (skymessage_test.py).
13838               	; 	WAIT
13839               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 3
13840               	; 		VPOKE #nav,95
13841               	; 		IF #nav > 9177 THEN
13842               	; 			#nsrc = #nav + 8
13843               	; 			VPOKE #nsrc,15
13844               	; 		END IF
13845               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
13846               	; 	NEXT nai
13847               	; 	#nsrc = 8488			' PPU row 9 col 8, the result box's TOP row
13848               	; 	IF #nav = 9182 THEN #nsrc = 8712	' GAME OVER's bottom row, 16
13849               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 15
13850               	; 		VPOKE #nsrc,CH_ECAR
13851               	; 		#nsrc = #nsrc + 1
13852               	; 	NEXT nai
13853               	; 	WAIT
13854               	; 	RETURN
13855               	;
13856               	; nes_attr:
13857               	; 	' nesb holds attributes only during draw_screen; flush before reuse by
13858               	; 	' escalator or marquee CHR uploads. One 64-byte copy fits one vblank.
13859               	; 	WAIT
13860               	; 	ASM JSR nes_attrs_put
13861               	; 	' Replace the title's SCORE/HI row with upper sky: 64+32 bytes,
13862               	; 	' two descriptors, 1444 cycles. Avoid 32 individual queued pokes.
13863               	; 	SCREEN blank_nes_row,0,96,32,1,32
13864               	; 	WAIT

13866               	; 	SCREEN floor_nes_row,0,736,32,1,32
13867               	; 	WAIT
13868               	; 	RETURN
13869               	; #endif

13949               	; 	' more like it -- four compares, four assignments and four jumps to walk a

14266               	; 	' every radar poke and HUD digit the pass had made. The copy then ran past

14274               	; 	' queued, and a WAIT per run made its twelve runs appear one frame at a
14275               	; 	' time -- a logo that visibly assembled itself.

14347               	;
14348               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
14349               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
14350               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
14351               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
14352               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
14353               	; 	'
14354               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
14355               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
14356               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
14357               	; 	'
14358               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
14359               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
14360               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
14361               	; 	'
14362               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
14363               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
14364               	; 	'
14365               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
14366               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
14367               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
14368               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
14369               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
14370               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
14371               	; 	'
14372               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
14373               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
14374               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
14375               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
14376               	; 	'
14377               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
14378               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
14379               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
14380               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
14381               	; bonus_count:

14524               	;
14525               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
14526               	; 	'
14527               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
14528               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
14529               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
14530               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
14531               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
14532               	; 	'
14533               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
14534               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
14535               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
14536               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
14537               	; 	' counting stops.
14538               	;
14539               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
14540               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
14541               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
14542               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
14543               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
14544               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
14545               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
14546               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
14547               	; 	'
14548               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
14549               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
14550               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14551               	;

14595               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
14596               	; 	'
14597               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
14598               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
14599               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
14600               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
14601               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
14602               	; 	'
14603               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
14604               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
14605               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
14606               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
14607               	; 	'
14608               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
14609               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
14610               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
14611               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
14612               	; 	'
14613               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
14614               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
14615               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
14616               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
14617               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
14618               	; 	'
14619               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
14620               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
14621               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
14622               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
14623               	; 	'
14624               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout
14625               	; 	' serve both cases. Losing a life draws three rows around it; losing the
14626               	; 	' last one draws two more ON TOP, so GAME OVER appears above the reason
14627               	; 	' rather than replacing it. Printing the reason at a different row for each
14628               	; 	' case would need `PRINT AT` with a variable, and every other PRINT in this
14629               	; 	' program uses a constant.

14639               	; 	' FLUSH THE PASS BEFORE DRAWING A BOX. PPUBUF accumulates for a whole loop
14640               	; 	' pass and is emptied by one NMI, so a message box -- sixty-four cells,
14641               	; 	' sixty-four single-byte descriptors -- was landing in the same vblank as
14642               	; 	' every radar poke and HUD digit the pass had made. The copy then ran past
14643               	; 	' the end of vblank and the tail was DISCARDED at the PPU: a box with
14644               	; 	' characters missing, and the cut moving from run to run, which is why it
14645               	; 	' read as intermittent corruption.
14646               	; 	'
14647               	; 	' One WAIT here empties the buffer; the box's own writes then self-pace,
14648               	; 	' because WRTVRM waits when PPUBUF fills. That is also why the TITLE never
14649               	; 	' needed this and must not have it: it is drawn at boot with nothing else
14650               	; 	' queued, and a WAIT per run made its twelve runs appear one frame at a
14651               	; 	' time -- a logo that visibly assembled itself.

14906               	;
14907               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
14908               	; 	'
14909               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
14910               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
14911               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
14912               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
14913               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
14914               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
14915               	; 	'
14916               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
14917               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
14918               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
14919               	; 	'
14920               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
14921               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
14922               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
14923               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
14924               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
14925               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
14926               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
14927               	; 	'
14928               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
14929               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
14930               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
14931               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
14932               	; 	'
14933               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
14934               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
14935               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
14936               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
14937               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
14938               	; 	'
14939               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
14940               	; 	' did not finish.
14941               	; pause_beat:
14942               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT

14994               	; 	' `SOUND ch,f,0` the last tone sustains for ever. And the second argument

15003               	; 	' written separately. Nothing else sets sfj, and if a jump and a plane
15004               	; 	' landed in one pass the last writer would win, which is academic: the

15019               	; 	' THE BIPLANE, which is TESTSOUNDS 5H with its tail trimmed off.
15020               	; 	'
15021               	; 	' 5H is the warble held low and long -- 235 Hz against 188, twelve half
15022               	; 	' cycles -- followed by 16 frames of 188 sitting there on its own. That
15023               	; 	' last step is the "extended beep" after the warble stops being a warble,
15024               	; 	' and it is the one part of the effect that is not doing any work: the
15025               	; 	' plane costs a KOP rather than nine seconds, and the round ends on the
15026               	; 	' spot, so there is nothing for a tail to decay over.
15027               	; 	'
15028               	; 	' IT RIDES THE JUMP'S WARBLE RATHER THAN BRINGING ITS OWN. The two share
15029               	; 	' their LOW note -- 5H's 596 and the jump's 595 are both 188 Hz, a quarter
15030               	; 	' of a hertz apart -- so the only thing that differs is the high note and
15031               	; 	' the length. One flag and one extra assignment buy the whole effect,
15032               	; 	' against sixty-odd bytes for a second warbler in a budget with eighty.

15376               	;
15377               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
15378               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
15379               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
15380               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
15381               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
15382               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
15383               	;
15384               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
15385               	; 	'
15386               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
15387               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
15388               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
15389               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
15390               	; 	'
15391               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
15392               	; 	'
15393               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
15394               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
15395               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
15396               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
15397               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
15398               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
15399               	; 	'
15400               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
15401               	; 	'
15402               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
15403               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
15404               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
15405               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
15406               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
15407               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
15408               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
15409               	; 	'
15410               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
15411               	; 	'
15412               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
15413               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
15414               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
15415               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
15416               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
15417               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
15418               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
15419               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
15420               	; 	'
15421               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
15422               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
15423               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
15424               	; 	'
15425               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
15426               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
15427               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
15428               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
15429               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
15430               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
15431               	; 	'
15432               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
15433               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
15434               	; 	'
15435               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
15436               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
15437               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
15438               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
15439               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
15440               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
15441               	; 	'
15442               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
15443               	; 	'
15444               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
15445               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
15446               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
15447               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
15448               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
15449               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not
15450               	; 	' back to 7.
15451               	; 	IF sfw > 13 THEN

15771 F84C 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F84E AE2A     
15772 F850 A684     	data wait
15773               	; 	GOTO life_finish
15774 F852 0460  28 	b @cvb_LIFE_FINISH
     F854 F830     
15775               	;
15776               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1 ON THE TI -- the
15777               	; 	' cart's ONE data bank, so the cart is 32 KB (DESIGN.md section 57).
15778               	; 	'
15779               	; 	' It holds the code that runs once or rarely (setup, the title, the 838
15780               	; 	' page, the random level generator, the music hooks) and the two LZSS
15781               	; 	' streams, which lz_setup and lz_probe unpack into lzbuf in RAM. Every
15782               	; 	' table the game reads is read from RAM. Power-on selects the bank once
15783               	; 	' and nothing ever switches it: a missed BANK SELECT returns bytes from
15784               	; 	' the wrong page with no error at build or run time, so the safest
15785               	; 	' number of switches is one.
15786               	; 	'
15787               	; 	' It was two banks and a 64 KB cart until the tables were compressed.
15788               	; 	' A second bank would double the cart again (five pages round up to
15789               	; 	' eight): assets/bankfill.py fails a bank image over 8,192 bytes.
15790               	; 	#if TI994A
15791               	; 	BANK 1
15792      07A8     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

16749               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- GAME MUSIC
16750               	; 	' CHASE (game_tune, genmusic.py) plays during a round on PLAY SIMPLE NO
16751               	; 	' DRUMS: TWO voices on channels 0 and 1 only. The TI effects split by
16752               	; 	' channel -- 0 the jump warble (swt), 1 hits and the escape (sht), 2
16753               	; 	' prizes/lives/tally, noise the footsteps -- so only jumps and hits
16754               	; 	' collide, and those DUCK the music: PLAY NONE freezes the player where
16755               	; 	' it is (it only clears music_mode; the song position is untouched), and
16756               	; 	' PLAY SIMPLE NO DRUMS resumes from the same note once they end.
16757               	; 	'
16758               	; 	' The test runs BEFORE sfx_tick writes anything, and counts the pending
16759               	; 	' latches (sfj/sfh/sfe) as well as the running counters, so the player
16760               	; 	' has let go of the channel before the effect's first write -- otherwise
16761               	; 	' the next vblank would stomp that first frame.
16762               	; 	'
16763               	; 	' Called from the main loop only, never from pause_beat: the round-end
16764               	; 	' pause is effects-only (pause_beat stops the music on entry).
16765               	; 	'
16766               	; 	' ON THE TI IT LIVES IN THE BANK: the fixed area's UNOPTIMISED first
16767               	; 	' pass had 156 bytes left and this body did not fit.

16779               	; 	' NES RAM IS FULL TO THE BYTE, so the NES keeps no gms/gmp/gmb: its whole
16780               	; 	' music state is nai -- 0 playing, 1 ducked, 2 not started. nai is NES
16781               	; 	' scratch that is idle here: the title's A toggle uses it (and treats 2
16782               	; 	' like a held A), and the round-end message boxes use it only after the
16783               	; 	' round's music is over and before music_stop sets it back to 2.
16784               	; 	IF nai = 2 THEN nai = 0 : PLAY SIMPLE NO DRUMS : PLAY game_tune
16785               	; 	' Same test as below, branching instead of setting gmb, plus the channel
16786               	; 	' owners the NES adds (the bugle on 0, the prize on 1 -- nes_apu.asm).
16787               	; 	' ONE TEST, NOT NINE. Every one of these is an unsigned byte, so "any is
16788               	; 	' non-zero" is their bitwise OR: one load and eight ORAs, about 35
16789               	; 	' bytes, where nine `IF x > 0 THEN GOTO` cost about 105 on the 6502 --
16790               	; 	' part of what let the NES title play the whole of STREET. (A bitwise OR

17254               	; 	' THE TITLE SITS ON DARK BLUE, AND THE BACKDROP IS THE ONLY WAY TO SAY SO.
17255               	; 	'
17256               	; 	' Palette index 0 is the UNIVERSAL backdrop -- every background palette's
17257               	; 	' entry 0 is the same colour, so it cannot be set per region the way the
17258               	; 	' sky and the store are. It was never written at all, which is why every
17259               	; 	' cell that maps to index 0 came out black, the title page included.
17260               	; 	'
17261               	; 	' Writing it here and putting it back in draw_screen costs two statements
17262               	; 	' and no art: the title is almost entirely index 0, so the backdrop IS its
17263               	; 	' background. draw_screen restores grey for buildings, pillars and the
17264               	; 	' scanner margins; black outlines now use palette index 2.
17265               	; 	PALETTE 0,1			' title backdrop
17266               	; 	PALETTE 9,1			' title paper in P2
17267               	; 	WAIT				' hide the clear and restore blue in the same vblank
17268               	; 	' AND EVERY BLOCK ON P2, because the font now has a PAPER.
17269               	; 	'
17270               	; 	' The title's text used to sit on index 0 and index 0 was this backdrop, so
17271               	; 	' it needed no attribute table at all and simply inherited whatever the
17272               	; 	' last game screen left. Now that paper is index 1, "FIRE TO START" would
17273               	; 	' take index 1 of each block it happens to cross -- the store's green under
17274               	; 	' one row, the sunset's orange under another.
17275               	; 	'
17276               	; 	' P2 is the palette that already fits: its index 1 is the same dark blue as
17277               	; 	' the backdrop, so the paper is invisible, and its index 3 is the yellow the
17278               	; 	' logo and the marquee lamps are drawn in. $AA is all four quadrants on P2.
17279               	; 	' draw_screen calls nes_attr and puts the game's own table back.
17280               	; 	#endif

17317               	;
17318               	;
17319               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
17320               	; 	'
17321               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
17322               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
17323               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
17324               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
17325               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
17326               	; 	'
17327               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
17328               	; 	'
17329               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
17330               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,

17406               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
17407               	; 	'
17408               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
17409               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
17410               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
17411               	; 	' picture.
17412               	; 	'
17413               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
17414               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
17415               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
17416               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
17417               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
17418               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
17419               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
17420               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
17421               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
17422               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
17423               	; 	' same picture.
17424               	; 	'
17425               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
17426               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
17427               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
17428               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
17429               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.
17430               	; 	bfr = bfr - 1
17431 6AF6 D020  34 	movb @cvb_BFR,r0
     6AF8 2086

     6AFC FF00

17448               	; 		' QUEUED, NOT BLANKED -- AND THIS IS WHAT MADE THE TITLE FLASH.
17449               	; 		'
17450               	; 		' nes_def turns rendering OFF and waits for a vblank the NMI
17451               	; 		' therefore never services, so the game's own WAIT then waits for
17452               	; 		' the one after: about two frames with the picture switched off.
17453               	; 		' Twice a marquee step, for ever, on the one screen the player
17454               	; 		' looks at longest. It reads as the whole title flashing, not as

17497               	; 		#if NES
17498               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
17499               	; 		'
17500               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
17501               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
17502               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
17503               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
17504               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
17505               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.
17506               	; 		'
17507               	; 		' So every step darkened two lamps and lit none, and the sign walked
17508               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
17509               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
17510               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
17511               	; 		'
17512               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
17513               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
17514               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
17515               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
17516               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.
17517               	; 		#nesb = #nesb + 16
17518               	; 		#nsrc = VARPTR bulb_off(0)
17519               	; 		nchr = bcode
17520               	; 		ncnt = 1
17521               	; 		ntab = 1
17522               	; 		#ncol = 0
17523               	; 		nink = 3
17524               	; 		GOSUB nes_escd			' queued -- see the note above
17525               	; 		#nesb = #nesb - 16

17755               	;
17756               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
17757               	; 	'
17758               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
17759               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
17760               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
17761               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
17762               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
17763               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
17764               	; 	'
17765               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
17766               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
17767               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
17768               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
17769               	; 	'
17770               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
17771               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
17772               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page
17773               	; 	' ======================================================================
17774               	; 	' A NEW GAME / A NEW KROOK
17775               	; 	' ======================================================================
17776               	;
17777               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- RUN ONCE
17778               	; 	' setup_font and init_tables run ONCE, at power-on, so on the TI they live
17779               	; 	' in the bank. They moved out of the fixed area to make room for the TI
17780               	; 	' music player (title music, ~1.2 KB of runtime): with it, the
17781               	; 	' UNOPTIMISED first assembly ran past >FFFF and xas99 rejected branches
17782               	; 	' before shortbranches.py could run (CLAUDE.md 3A, TI short-branch note).
17783               	; 	' On ColecoVision and NES this is ordinary code.
17784               	; setup_font:
17785               cvb_SETUP_FONT
17786               	; 	' Flicker stays OFF. CVBasic's is all-or-nothing -- it rotates all 32
17787               	; 	' slots, so Kelly would strobe too, and he is the one thing the player
17788               	; 	' must never lose. He is sprite 0 instead: the VDP drops the
17789               	; 	' HIGHEST-numbered sprites on an over-full scanline, so slot 0 is the
17790               	; 	' one slot that can never disappear.
17791               	; 	SPRITE FLICKER OFF

17798               	; 	#else

17800               	; 	' picture, and on a real set it is a good part of what the player sees --
17801               	; 	' left at the default black it made a hard frame around the shop. Dark blue
17802               	; 	' is the sky's own colour and the paper every piece of text sits on, so the

17815               	;
17816               	; 	#if NES
17817               	; 	' THE NES'S TWO STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCES, SETTLED ONCE, HERE.
17818               	; 	'
17819               	; 	' 1. WHERE THE PATTERNS LIVE. In 8x16 sprite mode the sprite pattern table
17820               	; 	'    is chosen by bit 0 of each OAM tile byte and the PPUCTRL bit is
17821               	; 	'    ignored -- and every pattern number in this game is a multiple of
17822               	; 	'    four, so that bit is always 0 and the sprites are nailed to $0000.
17823               	; 	'    nes_bgbank therefore moves the BACKGROUND to $1000 rather than trying
17824               	; 	'    to move the sprites, which also lands the background patterns at
17825               	; 	'    address 4096, exactly where the TMS bitmap mode's third screen third
17826               	; 	'    had them -- so the radar's pattern writes need a stride and nothing
17827               	; 	'    else.
17828               	; 	'
17829               	; 	' 2. COLOUR DOES NOT MAP AND IS NOT PRETENDED TO. The NES colours in 16x16
17830               	; 	'    attribute blocks; this game colours per character, two colours a
17831               	; 	'    cell. So the store is drawn in ONE ink and the actors get four
17832               	; 	'    palettes, picked by the low two bits of the colour argument the
17833               	; 	'    SPRITE statements already pass -- 1 (black) -> dark grey, 4/8 (blue)
17834               	; 	'    -> blue, 14 (grey) -> grey, 11/15 (skin, white) -> white. Nothing in
17835               	; 	'    the game source has to know.
17836               	; 	ASM JSR nes_bgbank
17837               	; 	ASM JSR nes_apuon
17838               	;
17839               	; 	' Grey is shared index 0 during gameplay. Other indices are per region.
17840               	; 	' gennescolor.py assigns P3 only to counter quadrants, retaining green
17841               	; 	' wall and gold floor colours. Fixtures with black outlines use P0.
17842               	; 	PALETTE 1,26			' P0: green, black, gold
17843               	; 	PALETTE 2,15			' black escalators and fixture outlines
17844               	; 	PALETTE 3,40
17845               	; 	PALETTE 5,1			' P1 HUD/upper skyline: blue, pink, gold
17846               	; 	PALETTE 6,36
17847               	; 	PALETTE 7,40
17848               	; 	PALETTE 9,38			' P2 lower skyline: orange, black, gold
17849               	; 	PALETTE 10,1			' skyline index 2: navy; the skyline boxes are gone (DESIGN 59)
17850               	; 	PALETTE 11,40
17851               	; 	PALETTE 13,26			' P3 counters: green, blue, gold
17852               	; 	PALETTE 14,1			' same navy in counter quadrants
17853               	; 	PALETTE 15,40
17854               	;
17855               	; 	' AND FOUR FOR THE ACTORS, which DO get one each because a sprite carries
17856               	; 	' its own palette number. nes_spal maps the TMS colour every SPRITE
17857               	; 	' statement already passes onto these four.
17858               	; 	PALETTE 17,18			' 0 -- blue   Kelly's trousers
17859               	; 	PALETTE 21,15			' 1 -- black  hats, Harry's stripes, the Kop's dot.
17860               	; 					' FIFTEEN, NOT ZERO: on this palette $0F is
17861               	; 					' black and $00 is a dark GREY, so every hat
17862               	; 					' and every stripe was coming out grey.
17863               	; 	PALETTE 22,23			' black sprite palette, index 2: brown suitcase outline
17864               	; 	PALETTE 25,39			' 2 -- skin   faces and the biplane
17865               	; 	PALETTE 26,16			' 2 colour 2 -- GREY, the lift car on the radar
17866               	; 	' AND THE BALL IS RED, which it already is on the TI: C_BALL is TMS 8,
17867               	; 	' medium red. nes_spal sends that to sprite palette 2, and palette 2's
17868               	; 	' colour ONE is the skin tone -- so on this machine the ball came out the
17869               	; 	' same pale orange as a face.
17870               	; 	'
17871               	; 	' A sprite here is ONE bitplane, so its pixels are whichever index the
17872               	; 	' upload writes and the OAM byte only chooses the palette. The lift car on
17873               	; 	' the radar already solved this: it is uploaded with `nink = 2` and reads
17874               	; 	' palette 2's second entry. The ball does the same with the THIRD, which
17875               	; 	' nothing else uses.
17876               	; 	PALETTE 27,22			' 2 colour 3 -- RED, the bouncing balls
17877               	; 	PALETTE 29,48			' 3 -- white  Harry, the carts, the lift car
17878               	;
17879               	; 	#endif
17880               	; 	#if TI994A
17881               	; 	#else
17882               	; 	nespw = 2			' NES/Coleco start on a 2-frame pass
17883               	; 	#endif
17884               	;
17885               	; 	' THE FONTS COME FROM lzbuf ON THE TI: lz_setup unpacked the setup
17886               	; 	' tables there at power-on, before this runs (DESIGN.md section 55).
17887               	; 	' If that ever goes wrong it goes wrong loudly -- the title's text is
17888               	; 	' garbage, immediately and unmistakably.
17889               	;
17890               	; 	#if NES
17891               	; 	' THE FONT IS SENT WITH A COLOUR TABLE SO ITS PAPER IS NOT THE BACKDROP.
17892               	; 	'
17893               	; 	' With `#ncol = 0` the uploader puts ink `nink` on index 0 -- the UNIVERSAL
17894               	; 	' backdrop, black in the game -- so every character of text sat in its own
17895               	; 	' black box. The score line was a black strip across the top of a blue sky.
17896               	; 	'
17897               	; 	' Index 0 cannot be set per region (it is one colour for the whole screen),
17898               	; 	' so the only way to give text a ground is to put its PAPER on another
17899               	; 	' index, and paper is written into the second bitplane when the character
17900               	; 	' is uploaded. Hence a table: $B4 is light yellow on dark blue, which
17901               	; 	' nes_inkmap sends to index 3 and index 1.
17902               	; 	'
17903               	; 	' ONE FONT, NOT TWO. The first attempt at this made a SECOND copy of the
17904               	; 	' font at codes 197.. so the HUD could differ from the message boxes, and
17905               	; 	' that was both unnecessary and impossible: in game the HUD and the boxes
17906               	; 	' are the same text and want the same treatment, and 197..207 is only
17907               	; 	' ELEVEN free codes -- 208 up is the radar canvas (genart's SCAN_FIRST),
17908               	; 	' which scan_wipe rewrites as raw pattern memory every frame. The 59-char
17909               	; 	' copy appeared to upload and was scribbled over from its twelfth character
17910               	; 	' on. See checkpat.py, which now knows the canvas owns those codes.
17911               	; 	'
17912               	; 	' What index 1 IS comes from the attribute table, per region: the HUD row
17913               	; 	' is on P1 (dark blue, below) and the store is on P0.
17914               	; 	#nsrc = VARPTR font_bits(0)
17915               	; 	nchr = 32
17916               	; 	ncnt = 59
17917               	; 	ntab = 1

17919               	; 	' on dark blue, ink index 3 on paper index 1, and which colours those are
17920               	; 	' is then the attribute table's business, per region. It used to be a
17921               	; 	' 472-byte table of that one value (nes_fcol), kept because "ROM is not
17922               	; 	' the scarce budget" -- on the NES it is. A #ncol under $100 is the
17923               	; 	' colour byte itself (assets/nes_chr.asm, nes_chrinkrow).

18193               	; 	' THE JUMP ARC IS A TABLE, not integration. That makes the 14 px apex a

18196               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a depends on the apex being exactly 14.
18197               	; 	'

18199               	; 	' frames that touched 14 for only four, which made every jump a timing
18200               	; 	' test rather than a decision -- you had to leave the ground on exactly
18201               	; 	' the right frame or clip the thing you were jumping. Widening the
18202               	; 	' plateau rather than raising the apex keeps the ball arithmetic in
18203               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a intact (the apex is what that depends on) while making the
18204               	; 	' window forgiving: the player still has to CHOOSE to jump, but no longer
18205               	; 	' has to be frame-perfect about it.

18241               	;
18242               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
18243               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
18244               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
18245               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
18246               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
18247               	; 	'
18248               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
18249               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
18250               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
18251               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
18252               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
18253               	; 	'
18254               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
18255               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
18256               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
18257               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
18258               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
18259               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
18260               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
18261               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
18262               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air
18263               	; 	' belonging to the floor BELOW it (see SLAB), which is right for three of
18264               	; 	' the four bars and wrong for the last one: below floor 0 there is no
18265               	; 	' floor, only the scanner, and the green read as a strip of shop with
18266               	; 	' nothing in it.
18267               	; 	'
18268               	; 	' NO NEW CHARACTER IS NEEDED, BECAUSE THE COLOUR TABLE HAS THREE COPIES
18269               	; 	' -- one per eight screen rows -- and the bands land such that each bar
18270               	; 	' sits in a different third:
18271               	; 	'
18272               	; 	'     band 0 roof   rows  1-5    bar row  5   third 0
18273               	; 	'     band 1        rows  6-10   bar row 10   third 1
18274               	; 	'     band 2        rows 11-15   bar row 15   third 1
18275               	; 	'     band 3 GROUND rows 16-20   bar row 20   third 2
18276               	; 	'
18277               	; 	' so recolouring SLAB in third 2 alone reaches the ground floor's bar and
18278               	; 	' nothing else. The same third also holds the scanner, but the scanner
18279               	; 	' does not use these characters. This is the same mechanism that once hid
18280               	; 	' a bug for months (CLAUDE.md 3A, the blanked-in-one-third note) used
18281               	; 	' deliberately for once.
18282               	; 	'
18283               	; 	' Only the three bottom lines change, and only their BACKGROUND: SLAB has
18284               	; 	' no ink there and SLABE's brick keeps its grey.

19083               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
19084               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
19085               	; 	' being small sprites.
19086               	; 	'
19087               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
19088               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
19089               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
19090               	; 	'
19091               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
19092               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
19093               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).

19871               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
19872               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
19873               	; 	'
19874               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
19875               	; 	' blit is
19876               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
19877               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
19878               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
19879               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
19880               	; 	'

20981               	; 	' big-endian (offset << 6 | length - 3), offset 1..1023 back into the

20983               	; 	' the output length (it stops there, so a stream's padding is never read).
20984               	; 	' R1-R9 only: R10 is CVBasic's stack pointer and R11 its return link.
20985               	; 	' It lives in BANK 1 with its stream, which must be selected (power-on
20986               	; 	' selects it before calling lz_probe), and needs no fixed-area room.
